content: Torticollis, also known as wry neck or loxia, is a condition characterized by an abnormal twisting of the neck, where the head tilts to one side while the chin rotates to the opposite side. Symptoms of Torticollis: The range of motion of the head is significantly restricted. Patients may experience headaches. Tremors of the head can occur. Pain in the neck is a common symptom. One shoulder may appear higher than the other. The neck muscles may feel stiff. Swelling of the neck muscles may be observed, and in some cases, this swelling is present at birth. Causes of Torticollis: Torticollis can be inherited, resulting from specific genetic mutations. It can also be acquired due to damage to the nervous system or muscles. When the cause is unknown, the condition is referred to as idiopathic torticollis. Torticollis can manifest during childhood or adulthood. Congenital torticollis, present at birth, may result from improper positioning of the fetus's head in the womb or injury to the neck muscles or blood supply during fetal development. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: You should contact a healthcare provider if symptoms persist despite treatment or if new symptoms arise. Torticollis that develops following an injury or during an illness may indicate a serious condition and requires immediate medical attention. Diagnosis: A physical examination typically reveals a visible shortening of the neck muscles, with the head tilting toward the affected side and the chin pointing to the opposite side. In severe cases, the entire head may be pulled and rotated to one side. An electromyogram (EMG) may be performed in mild cases to identify the specific muscles that are most affected. Treatment Options: For congenital torticollis, treatment involves stretching the shortened neck muscles. Passive stretching and proper positioning are effective treatments for infants and young children, especially if initiated within the first three months of life. If conservative treatments fail, surgical correction of the neck muscle may be considered during the preschool years. For acquired torticollis, treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause. Heat application, cervical spine traction, and massage can help alleviate head and neck pain. Stretching exercises and neck braces may reduce muscle spasms. Medications such as the anticholinergic drug baclofen are sometimes used. Botulinum toxin injections can provide temporary relief, but repeated injections every three months are typically required. Surgery is rarely performed for acquired torticollis. Prognosis: The condition is often easier to treat in infants and children. However, if left untreated and allowed to become chronic, nerve root compression in the neck may lead to numbness and tingling. Chronic stimulation and exercise of the affected muscle may cause it to enlarge (hypertrophy). Botulinum toxin injections frequently offer significant symptom relief. Possible Complications: Persistent muscle tension may lead to swelling of the affected muscles. Compression of nerve roots in the neck can result in neurological symptoms. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent torticollis. However, early intervention and treatment can help prevent the condition from worsening.
